Content

Magnetic Effect of an Electric Current

  • The magnetic effect of electric current is the phenomenon where an electric current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around it. This field can exert force on other magnets or moving charges.
  • E.g. Deflection of a compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire.
  • The strength of the magnetic field increases with the amount of current flowing through the wire.
  • The direction of magnetic field changes due to a change in direction of current in the wire.
  • Hans Christian Oersted discovered the magnetic effect of electric current in 1820.

Magnetic Field Lines

  • The magnetic field created by a current-carrying wire is a force field that influences other magnets and moving charges.
  • When iron filings are scattered around a magnet, they become temporary magnets through magnetic induction and align end-to-end along the magnetic field lines. The filings clump more densely near the poles, showing that the magnetic field is the strongest near the poles. This pattern of filings gives a clear visual impression of the magnetic field around the magnet.
  • Like poles repel each other and Unlike poles attract each other.

Properties of a Magnetic Field Lines

  1. 1. They always go from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.
  2. 2. Inside the magnet, they go from the south pole to the north pole, forming closed loops.
  3. 3. The closer the lines are, the stronger the magnetic field.
  4. 4. Magnetic field lines never cross each other. If they intersect, there will be two direction of magnetic field lines, which is not possible.
  5. 5. They show the direction and strength of the magnetic field.

Magnetic Field Due to Straight Current Carrying Conductor

  • The magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor consists of concentric circles centered on the wire.
  • These circular magnetic field lines form around the wire when electric current flows through it.
  • The direction of the field can be found using the Right-Hand Thumb Rule → if you point your right thumb in the direction of the current, your fingers will curl in the direction of the magnetic field lines.

(Diagram: Right-Hand Thumb Rule — thumb points in current direction I, fingers curl showing field B)

  • Magnetic Field ∝ 1 / Distance → As you go farther from the wire, the magnetic field becomes weaker.
  • Magnetic Field ∝ Current → A stronger current produces a stronger magnetic field.
  • Change in Current Direction → Change in Magnetic Field Direction → If current flows downward, the magnetic field become clockwise. If the current flows upward, the magnetic field lines become anti-clockwise.
  • Increasing the number of loops/turns in a current-carrying wire coil strengthens the magnetic field. E.g. On doubling the number of turns the magnetic field also doubles

Maxwell's Screw Rule

  • Maxwell's screw rule is a way to find the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor.

Rule:

  • Imagine turning a right-handed screw (or corkscrew) in the direction of the current. Then, the direction in which the screw rotates gives the direction of the magnetic field lines.

Ampere's Law

Ampere's Law essentially states that "The line integral of the magnetic field around a close loop is proportional to the total current passing through the loop". It is used to calculate the magnetic field in various configurations, such as around straight wires or solenoids.

∮ B.dl = μ₀ I

Magnetic Field Current Due to a Current Carrying Solenoid

  • The magnetic field inside a solenoid is uniform and strongest in the center.
  • For a long, ideal solenoid (where the length is much greater than the radius), the magnetic field outside is considered to be zero.
  • A solenoid behaves like a magnet when a current flows through it because it creates a magnetic field that resembles that of a bar magnet.
  • When current flows through the coils of a solenoid, each turn of the coil generates its own magnetic field. These fields combine to create a strong, relatively uniform magnetic field inside the solenoid.
  • If the direction of current is reversed, the direction of magnetic field is also reversed.

(Diagram: Solenoid with Battery and Key showing Magnetic field of solenoid)

Electromagnet

  • An electromagnet is a temporary magnet, meaning it only exhibits magnetic properties when an electric current is flowing through its coil, and loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.
  • If a soft iron core is placed inside this coil, the magnetic field from the coil will induce magnetism in the soft iron. The induced magnetism is temporary. As long as the current flows, the soft iron remains magnetized. Once the current stops, the soft iron loses its magnetism.

(Diagram: Simple Electromagnet — coil wire, iron core, battery)

Force on a Current Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field

  • A current-carrying conductor experiences a force when placed in a magnetic field. This force is caused by the interaction between the magnetic field generated by the current in the conductor and the external magnetic field.

(Diagram: Case 1 — θ = 90°; Case 2 — θ = 0°)

F = I(L × B)

Where:

  • F: Magnetic force on the conductor.
  • I: Current in the conductor.
  • L: Length of the conductor in the direction of current.
  • B: Magnetic field.
  • If the angle between L and B is θ, then: F = ILB sin θ.

Conditions:

  • The maximum force is experienced when the angle is 90°, because the sin θ becomes 1, which is the maximum value.
  • When the angle is 0°, the force experienced is zero because sin θ is zero.
  • When the angle is 180°, the force experienced is also zero because sin θ is again zero.

Fleming's Left Hand Rule

  • Fleming's Left Hand Rule states that "If you extend your left thumb, index finger, and middle finger at right angles to each other, the thumb points in the direction of the force, the index finger points in the direction of the magnetic field, and the middle finger points in the direction of the current".
  • It is used to determine the direction of force (motion) on a current carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
  • E.g. Motor (electrical energy is converted to mechanical energy) works on the principle of Fleming's Left Hand Rule.

Fleming's Right Hand Rule

  • Fleming's Right-Hand Rule helps determine the direction of induced current in a generator (mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy). It uses the right hand where the thumb indicates the direction of motion, the first finger (forefinger) indicates the magnetic field, and the second finger (middle finger) indicates the direction of induced current.

Electromagnetic Induction

  • Electromagnetic Induction is a phenomenon in which current is produced because of voltage production (electromotive force) due to a changing magnetic field.
  • This either happens when a conductor is placed in a moving magnetic field (when using an AC power source) or when a conductor is constantly moving in a stationary magnetic field.
  • Electromagnetic induction was discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831.
  • When the bar magnet is pushed towards the coil, the pointer in the galvanometer deflects.
  • The relative motion between the magnet and the coil is responsible for generation of electric current in the coil.

Short Circuit

  • Short Circuit is caused due to breaking of insulation of wires, forming the contact between live wire and neutral wire.
  • During a short circuit, the current in a circuit increases abruptly and significantly. This is because a short circuit creates a very low resistance path, allowing a large amount of current to flow.
  • Live wire: red colour (220V)
  • Neutral wire: black colour (0V)

#### DC vs AC

DCAC
Current flows only in one directionCurrent changes its direction every 1/100th of a second
  • A Rectifier converts AC to DC.
  • An Inverter converts DC to AC.
